label: Out on errands
rationale: Running errands: grab some cash, is the shop open yet, has it closed, wait your turn.
mixUps: A shop's aiteru means 'open', not 'free' as in ashita aiteru?; shimatteru is 'closed'. orosu is cash from the ATM, not toru. junban o matsu is waiting your turn, while standing in the queue itself is narabu.

targets.trap: Not okane o toru, which sounds like taking someone's money. Cash from an ATM is orosu, 'bring down'. Casual dasu also works.
targets.use: What you say on the way to the ATM or konbini: chotto okane oroshite kuru, okane orosanakya. The o usually drops.
targets.notes: hikidasu is the formal word; ATM voice prompts and bank staff say ohikidashi.

example.ja: ちょっとお金下ろしてくる
example.english: I'm just going to grab some cash.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお金を下ろしてきます
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to grab some cash.

targets.verbSense: of a door or shop: open, by itself
targets.trap: About the shop itself, use aiteru: ano mise mou aiteru?. akeru is what the staff do, so aketemasu ka? fits only when you ask the staff. yatteru also works. mise o hiraku is starting a new shop.
targets.use: Almost always aiteru (is open), in questions about hours: kono mise nanji made aiteru?. Plain aku is the moment it opens: juuji ni aku. yatteru (is open for business) is just as common: nanji made yatteru?
targets.notes: mise o akeru = the staff open up; mise o hiraku = start a new shop. A door opening uses the same verb: doa ga aku.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa mou aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの店はもう開いてますか？

targets.verbSense: of a door or shop: close, by itself
targets.trap: For the shop's own state, use shimaru: mou shimatteru = it's already closed. shimeru is the staff closing up, so nanji ni shimemasu ka? fits only when you ask the staff. Casual owaru also works.
targets.use: Mostly shimatteru (is closed) and shimatchau (is about to close): hayaku ikanai to shimatchau yo. Plain shimaru gives the time: kuji ni shimaru.
targets.notes: Closing for good is mise o tatamu, or tsubureru (go bust). Sounds like shimau (put away; the -chau ending): mou shimatta can mean 'I already put it away', and shimatta! alone means 'oops'. Context decides.

example.ja: あの店、もう閉まってるよ

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa mou shimattemasu yo
examplePolite.ja: あの店はもう閉まってますよ

targets.use: Said to kids (chanto junban matte ne) and as a pointed remark to someone pushing in: minna junban matteru n desu kedo. The noun junban machi is common too (ima sanjuppun junban machi da tte), and when your turn comes it's junban ga kita, or just ban: tsugi, dare no ban?
targets.notes: Pushing in is warikomi: warikomi shinaide.

example.ja: ちゃんと順番待ってね。

examplePolite.romaji: chanto junban o matte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと順番を待ってくださいね。

reviewPool.english: sound comes out (of a TV, speaker, phone)
